II-21.explain: JIA is a diagnosis of exclusion with two time rules: it starts before the 16th birthday and must persist at least 6 weeks, which rules out transient reactive or viral arthritis.

checks.q: Minimum duration of arthritis required to diagnose JIA?
checks.why: At least 6 weeks; shorter episodes are usually reactive/viral arthritis.

II-21.explain: Subtypes are defined by how many joints and which serology; the commonest, oligoarticular, hits young ANA-positive girls.
II-21.hook: Oligo = 'Only a few joints, Often little girls'.

checks.q: Most common JIA subtype?
checks.why: Oligoarticular is ~50% of JIA, typically young ANA+ girls; RF+ polyarticular is rare.

II-21.explain: Cytokines drive synovial overgrowth (pannus) that erodes cartilage; systemic JIA is autoinflammatory (IL-1/IL-6) so autoantibodies are absent. In MAS, fibrinogen is consumed so ESR paradoxically falls.
II-21.hook: MAS clue: ferritin rockets, ESR drops.

checks.q: Inflamed synovial tissue that erodes cartilage in JIA is called?
checks.why: Pannus = hyperplastic synovium; tophi are gout, osteophytes are OA.

checks.q: Which cytokines chiefly drive systemic JIA?
checks.why: sJIA is autoinflammatory, IL-1/IL-6 driven, hence anakinra/tocilizumab work; ANA and RF negative.

checks.q: In macrophage activation syndrome, the ESR typically does what?
checks.why: ESR falls because fibrinogen is consumed, despite a raging cytokine storm.

II-21.explain: Chronic hyperaemia around an inflamed joint stimulates the growth plate (limb overgrowth). ANA+ oligo disease causes a painless uveitis, so children never complain. Systemic JIA looks like infection: daily fever spikes with an evanescent rash.
II-21.hook: sJIA: fever spikes once daily, rash comes with the fever.

checks.q: Local growth effect of chronic knee arthritis in a child?
checks.why: Hyperaemia stimulates the physis, causing overgrowth and leg-length discrepancy.

checks.q: Typical eye complication of ANA-positive oligoarticular JIA?
checks.why: Chronic anterior uveitis is painless and white, so it needs screening, unlike HLA-B27 acute uveitis.

checks.q: Fever pattern typical of systemic JIA?
checks.why: Quotidian: one or two daily spikes back to normal, with salmon-pink rash.

II-21.explain: No test proves JIA; serology predicts course (ANA → eye risk, RF/anti-CCP → erosions). Leukaemia and sepsis must be excluded first. Screening intensity follows uveitis risk.
II-21.hook: Night pain + cytopenia = leukaemia until proven otherwise.

checks.q: In JIA, a positive ANA mainly predicts what?
checks.why: ANA marks uveitis risk; RF/anti-CCP predict erosive disease.

checks.q: Which feature points to leukaemia rather than JIA?
checks.why: Night pain, cytopenias and high LDH suggest leukaemia; stiffness easing with activity suggests JIA.

checks.q: Slit-lamp screening interval for ANA-positive oligoarticular JIA?
checks.why: Every 3 months because uveitis is silent; the eye is not red.

II-21.explain: Treatment escalates: NSAIDs, joint steroid injection, then weekly methotrexate, then biologics. sJIA goes straight to IL-1/IL-6 blockade. MAS, the most serious complication, needs urgent high-dose steroids.
II-21.hook: Ladder: NSAID → inject → MTX weekly → biologic.

checks.q: Standard dosing schedule of methotrexate in JIA?
checks.why: Once weekly with folic acid; daily dosing is a dangerous error.

checks.q: First-line biologic for systemic JIA?
checks.why: IL-1 (anakinra) or IL-6 (tocilizumab) blockade; anti-TNF works poorly in sJIA.

checks.q: Most serious complication of JIA?
checks.why: MAS (official answer), treated with IV methylprednisolone, anakinra, ciclosporin.

II-22.explain: Hepatitis viruses A to E primarily target the liver, unlike EBV or CMV which involve it as part of systemic infection.

checks.q: Which viruses are the classic hepatotropic hepatitis viruses?
checks.why: Hepatitis A-E primarily infect hepatocytes; EBV/CMV cause hepatitis secondarily.

II-22.explain: Route predicts chronicity: gut-spread A and E clear; blood-borne B, C, D can persist. Non-viral mimics such as paracetamol and Wilson must be considered.
II-22.hook: Vowels (A, E) from the bowels; consonants chronic.

checks.q: Which hepatitis viruses are faecal-oral and self-limiting?
checks.why: A and E (vowels, bowels) do not become chronic; B, C, D are blood/vertical.

checks.q: Which metabolic disease can mimic acute viral hepatitis in older children?
checks.why: Wilson disease (with paracetamol, autoimmune, EBV, CMV) is a key differential.

II-22.explain: The damage is immune: cytotoxic T cells kill infected hepatocytes, releasing transaminases. Neonates are tolerant to HBV, so they rarely clear it.
II-22.hook: The younger the host, the more chronic HBV becomes.

checks.q: What directly kills hepatocytes in acute viral hepatitis?
checks.why: Cytotoxic T cells cause the injury, so ALT/AST rise into the thousands.

checks.q: Classic stool colour in hepatitis with cholestasis?
checks.why: Conjugated bilirubin fails to reach the gut: pale stools, dark urine, itch.

checks.q: Proportion of perinatal HBV infections that become chronic?
checks.why: ~90% perinatally vs ~5% in adults, due to immune tolerance in neonates.

II-22.explain: Systemic prodrome precedes jaundice; young children with hepatitis A often never turn yellow, which helps the virus spread silently.
II-22.hook: Little kids with HAV: sick but not yellow.

checks.q: How does hepatitis A usually present in young children?
checks.why: Mostly anicteric in young children; jaundice is more common in older children/adults.

II-22.explain: Serology identifies the virus (IgM = acute). Severity is judged by synthetic function: an INR that vitamin K does not correct means true liver failure.

checks.q: Which marker pair defines acute hepatitis B?
checks.why: HBsAg with IgM anti-HBc = acute B; anti-HBs indicates immunity.

checks.q: Best marker of severity in acute hepatitis?
options: INR not corrected by vitamin K
checks.why: INR reflects synthetic failure; ALT height does not track severity.

checks.q: PALF INR threshold without encephalopathy?
checks.why: INR ≥ 2.0 without encephalopathy, or ≥ 1.5 with encephalopathy.

II-22.explain: Acute hepatitis needs support only; antivirals are reserved for chronic infection. Newborns of HBsAg+ mothers get active plus passive immunisation fast.
II-22.hook: Baby of HBsAg+ mum: vaccine + HBIG in 12 h.

checks.q: Mainstay of treatment for acute viral hepatitis?
checks.why: Supportive; admit if INR raised, hypoglycaemic or encephalopathic.

checks.q: Antiviral used for chronic hepatitis B?
checks.why: Entecavir/tenofovir for HBV; sofosbuvir-based DAAs are for HCV.

checks.q: Deadline for HBV vaccine + HBIG in a newborn of an HBsAg+ mother?
checks.why: Within 12 hours of birth to prevent vertical transmission.

II-23.explain: Children rarely transmit TB; a child with TB means a recently infected household adult is the source, so contact tracing is essential.
II-23.hook: Child with TB = find the coughing adult.

checks.q: Childhood TB usually reflects what?
checks.why: Paediatric TB is a sentinel of recent adult transmission.

II-23.explain: Cavitary adult lungs shed huge bacillary loads as droplet nuclei. Immature or impaired immunity (infants, HIV, malnutrition, measles) favours progression.

checks.q: Typical source of TB infection in a child?
checks.why: Adults with cavities shed droplet nuclei; children with primary TB are rarely infectious.

checks.q: Which age group is at highest risk of progressing to TB disease?
checks.why: Under 2 years, along with HIV, malnutrition and measles.

II-23.explain: Bacilli seed a lung focus and drain to hilar nodes (Ghon complex); cord factor triggers TNF-driven granulomas. Infants cannot contain it, so it disseminates.

checks.q: Ghon complex consists of what?
checks.why: Ghon focus plus ipsilateral hilar lymphadenopathy is primary TB.

checks.q: Which mycobacterial factor drives granuloma formation via TNF-α?
checks.why: Cord factor stimulates macrophages to release TNF-α; sulfatides block phagolysosome fusion.

checks.q: Which forms of TB are typical under 2 years of age?
checks.why: Infants spread TB haematogenously → miliary TB and TB meningitis.

II-23.explain: Primary infection is usually silent; disease gives prolonged cough with constitutional symptoms. Extrapulmonary sites include nodes and spine.

checks.q: Cough duration that should raise suspicion of TB?
checks.why: Cough >2 weeks with fever, night sweats, weight loss.

checks.q: Pott disease is TB of which site?
checks.why: Pott = vertebral TB; scrofula = cervical lymphadenitis.

II-23.explain: Children are paucibacillary, so diagnosis combines contact history, immune tests and CXR. IGRA uses antigens absent from BCG. Swallowed sputum is sampled from the stomach.
II-23.hook: TST cut-offs 5-10-15: high, intermediate, low risk.

checks.q: Advantage of IGRA over tuberculin skin test?
checks.why: IGRA antigens are absent from BCG, so fewer false positives.

checks.q: TST induration positive in a low-risk child?
checks.why: ≥15 mm low risk, ≥10 intermediate, ≥5 high risk (HIV, contact).

checks.q: Classic sample to find TB in young children who cannot expectorate?
checks.why: Children swallow sputum overnight; gastric aspirates or induced sputum go to Xpert/culture.

II-23.explain: Four drugs kill all bacillary populations in the 2-month intensive phase; two continue for 4 months. Isoniazid depletes B6. Young contacts get prophylaxis because they progress quickly.

checks.q: Standard duration of continuation phase (HR) for pulmonary TB?
checks.why: 2 months HRZ(E) then 4 months HR = 6 months total.

checks.q: Total treatment duration for TB meningitis?
checks.why: 12 months plus corticosteroids to reduce neurological sequelae.

checks.q: Which contacts get preventive therapy even if tests are negative?
checks.why: Under-5s progress fast and tests may be falsely negative early.

II-24.explain: Humoral defects mean B cells or antibodies fail; the four classics differ in which step breaks (maturation, differentiation, IgA, class switching).

checks.q: Which is a primary antibody (B-cell) deficiency?
checks.why: XLA is a B-cell defect; DiGeorge is T-cell, CGD is phagocytic.

II-24.explain: XLA is a kinase defect blocking B-cell maturation in boys; CVID blocks plasma-cell formation. Hyper-IgM is actually a T-cell signalling defect (CD40L).
II-24.hook: Bruton = Boys, BTK, no B cells.

checks.q: Gene mutated in X-linked agammaglobulinaemia?
checks.why: BTK (Bruton tyrosine kinase); CD40L = hyper-IgM, WAS = Wiskott-Aldrich.

checks.q: Defective molecule in X-linked hyper-IgM syndrome?
checks.why: CD40L on T helper cells is needed to signal class switching.

II-24.explain: Without IgG, encapsulated bacteria are not opsonised. Maternal IgG protects for about 6 months, so infections start after that.
II-24.hook: Maternal IgG fades at 6 months → infections begin.

checks.q: Why do encapsulated bacteria thrive in XLA?
checks.why: Capsules resist phagocytosis unless opsonised by IgG.

checks.q: When do infections typically start in XLA?
checks.why: Transplacental maternal IgG wanes around 6 months.

II-24.explain: Recurrent sinopulmonary infection scars airways. XLA has no lymphoid tissue to see. IgA deficiency is common and mild but anti-IgA antibodies cause transfusion reactions.

checks.q: Classic viral complication of XLA?
checks.why: Enteroviruses need antibody for clearance, causing chronic meningoencephalitis.

checks.q: Examination finding typical of XLA?
checks.why: No B cells → no germinal centres → absent tonsils and lymph nodes.

checks.q: Classic hazard in selective IgA deficiency?
checks.why: Anti-IgA antibodies react to IgA in donor blood.

II-24.explain: Measure levels first, then function (vaccine responses), then cells (CD19) and genes.

checks.q: In selective IgA deficiency, IgG and IgM levels are?
checks.why: Isolated low IgA with normal IgG and IgM.

checks.q: When are post-booster vaccine titres checked?
checks.why: Titres before and 4-6 weeks after the booster test functional antibody.

checks.q: Flow cytometry finding in XLA?
checks.why: B cells (CD19) are absent; T cells are normal.

II-24.explain: Replace the missing antibody regularly, treat infections early. IgA deficiency gets no IgG replacement; it needs washed products.

checks.q: Usual IVIG replacement interval?
checks.why: IV every 3-4 weeks or subcutaneous weekly.

checks.q: Which vaccines are contraindicated in XLA?
checks.why: Live vaccines (e.g. oral polio) can cause disease without antibody.

checks.q: Blood products for IgA-deficient patients should be?
checks.why: Washed (IgA-depleted) products avoid anti-IgA anaphylaxis.

II-25.explain: T cells help B cells, so T-cell defects nearly always become combined immunodeficiencies.
II-25.hook: No T help, no B work.

checks.q: Why are T-cell defects usually 'combined'?
checks.why: B cells need T helper signals to make effective antibody.

II-25.explain: Most SCID is X-linked loss of the shared cytokine receptor gamma chain; others are ADA or RAG. DiGeorge is a chromosome deletion.

checks.q: Commonest cause of SCID?
checks.why: X-linked common γ-chain (IL2RG) defect is the commonest form.

checks.q: Genetic lesion in DiGeorge syndrome?
checks.why: 22q11.2 deletion; 7q11.23 is Williams syndrome.

II-25.explain: Without T cells there is no defence against intracellular organisms. ADA lets toxic dATP accumulate; RAG blocks receptor rearrangement. DiGeorge is a pouch development defect.

checks.q: Which organisms are poorly controlled without T cells?
checks.why: T cells control intracellular pathogens; encapsulated bacteria reflect antibody defects.

checks.q: Toxic metabolite in ADA deficiency?
checks.why: dATP accumulates and is toxic to lymphocytes.

checks.q: Which pharyngeal pouches are abnormal in DiGeorge?
checks.why: 3rd/4th pouches → thymic and parathyroid hypoplasia.

II-25.explain: SCID presents in early infancy with opportunists. DiGeorge shows its pouch and heart defects; WAS has a classic triad.

checks.q: Typical opportunistic pneumonia in SCID infants?
checks.why: Pneumocystis plus thrush, chronic viral diarrhoea and FTT in the first months.

checks.q: Neonatal metabolic finding in DiGeorge?
checks.why: Parathyroid hypoplasia → hypocalcaemic seizures/tetany.

checks.q: Platelet feature in Wiskott-Aldrich syndrome?
checks.why: Thrombocytopenia with small platelets; giant platelets suggest Bernard-Soulier.

II-25.explain: SCID shows lymphopenia and no thymus. Newborn screening counts TRECs, DNA circles made during T-cell receptor rearrangement.
II-25.hook: Low TRECs = no new T cells.

checks.q: Chest X-ray clue in SCID?
checks.why: No thymus is visible; the sail sign is a normal thymus.

checks.q: Newborn screening test for SCID?
checks.why: T-cell receptor excision circles reflect thymic output; NBT is for CGD.

II-25.explain: Protect (isolation, irradiated CMV-negative blood, no live vaccines), prevent PJP, then cure with early stem cell transplant.

checks.q: Required blood product modification in SCID?
checks.why: Irradiation prevents graft-versus-host disease; CMV-negative avoids infection.

checks.q: PJP prophylaxis in SCID?
checks.why: TMP-SMX prevents PJP; fluconazole is antifungal for Candida.

checks.q: Curative treatment for SCID?
checks.why: HSCT, >90% success if done before 3.5 months.

II-26.explain: All three complement pathways converge on C3, which coats (opsonises), recruits inflammatory cells and builds the membrane attack complex.

checks.q: Where do all complement pathways converge?
checks.why: C3 is the convergence point; classical begins with C1.

II-26.explain: Deficiency can affect any component; C1-inhibitor deficiency is autosomal dominant and causes hereditary angioedema.

checks.q: Which complement deficiency is terminal pathway?
checks.why: C5-C9 are terminal; C1q, C2, C4 are early classical.

checks.q: Inheritance of C1-inhibitor deficiency?
checks.why: AD → hereditary angioedema.

II-26.explain: Early classical components clear immune complexes, so their loss causes lupus. No MAC means Neisseria survive. No C1-inhibitor lets bradykinin leak vessels.

checks.q: Early classical complement deficiency predisposes to what?
checks.why: Immune complexes are not cleared → lupus-like disease.

checks.q: C5-C9 deficiency predisposes to recurrent infection with?
checks.why: No MAC → no lysis of Neisseria.

checks.q: Mediator causing swelling in hereditary angioedema?
checks.why: Bradykinin excess, so antihistamines do not work.

II-26.explain: Presentation maps to the missing component: lupus, pyogenic or meningococcal infection, aHUS, or non-itchy angioedema.

checks.q: Classic infection pattern in terminal complement deficiency?
checks.why: Recurrent Neisseria meningitidis infections.

checks.q: Factor H defect causes which disorder?
checks.why: Uncontrolled alternative pathway on endothelium → aHUS.

checks.q: Which feature is absent in hereditary angioedema?
checks.why: HAE swelling is non-itchy with no urticaria, unlike allergic angioedema.

II-26.explain: CH50/AH50 screen pathway function; C4 falls during HAE. Unusual meningococcal disease warrants a complement screen.

checks.q: Screening test of classical complement pathway function?
checks.why: CH50 = classical; AH50 = alternative.

checks.q: When should a child with meningococcal disease get complement tests?
checks.why: A second episode or unusual serogroup suggests complement deficiency.

checks.q: Screening test for hereditary angioedema?
checks.why: C4 is low; then confirm with C1-inhibitor level and function.

II-26.explain: Vaccinate against encapsulated organisms. Eculizumab blocks C5 so recipients must be meningococcal-vaccinated. HAE needs C1-inhibitor or bradykinin blockade.

checks.q: Treatment for atypical HUS?
checks.why: Anti-C5 eculizumab; needs meningococcal vaccination first.

checks.q: Why must eculizumab patients get meningococcal vaccine?
checks.why: C5 blockade prevents MAC formation, mimicking terminal deficiency.

checks.q: Acute treatment of hereditary angioedema attack?
checks.why: C1-inhibitor concentrate or icatibant; adrenaline/antihistamines/steroids don't work.

II-27.explain: HIV targets CD4 cells; in children most infection comes from the mother, mainly during delivery.

checks.q: Most common timing of vertical HIV transmission?
checks.why: Most vertical transmission occurs intrapartum.

II-27.explain: Mother-to-child routes dominate in infants; adolescents acquire it like adults.

checks.q: Main route of HIV acquisition in adolescents?
checks.why: Adolescents acquire HIV sexually or through injecting drugs.

II-27.explain: gp120 binds CD4 plus a co-receptor; gp41 fuses. Children progress faster because their thymus and immune system are immature and viral loads are high.

checks.q: Co-receptor used early by macrophage-tropic HIV?
checks.why: CCR5 early (macrophages); CXCR4 later (T cells).

checks.q: Main immunological consequence of HIV infection?
checks.why: CD4 depletion with chronic immune activation.

checks.q: Compared with adults, untreated HIV in children progresses?
checks.why: Developing thymus and higher viral set points speed progression.

II-27.explain: Paediatric HIV looks like failure to thrive with lymphoid hyperplasia. A 3-6 month infant with severe hypoxic pneumonia should prompt PJP.

checks.q: Which gland swelling is typical of paediatric HIV?
checks.why: Parotid swelling with lymphadenopathy and hepatosplenomegaly.

checks.q: Infant of 3-6 months with HIV and severe hypoxia: likely?
checks.why: PJP peaks at 3-6 months with marked hypoxia; LIP is slower and older.

II-27.explain: Maternal IgG crosses the placenta and persists up to 18 months, so infants need virological tests.
II-27.hook: Under 18 months: test the virus, not antibody.

checks.q: Diagnostic test for HIV in a 6-month-old?
checks.why: Maternal IgG persists, so PCR is needed under 18 months.

checks.q: From what age are antibody/antigen tests reliable?
checks.why: After 18 months maternal antibody has gone.

II-27.explain: Prevention bundle drops transmission below 1%. All children start ART at diagnosis. Co-trimoxazole prevents PJP; rifampicin induces PI metabolism, so rifabutin is used.

checks.q: Neonatal drug for HIV prophylaxis?
checks.why: Neonatal zidovudine plus maternal ART and avoiding breastfeeding → <1%.

checks.q: When is ART started in a child with HIV?
checks.why: At diagnosis regardless of CD4: 2 NRTIs + dolutegravir.

checks.q: Which vaccine is avoided in HIV-infected infants?
checks.why: BCG is live and can disseminate; co-trimoxazole from 4-6 weeks.

II-28.explain: Opportunists exploit a specific hole in immunity, so knowing the defect predicts the bug.

checks.q: What best predicts the likely opportunistic organism?
checks.why: The immune defect predicts the organism.

II-28.explain: Causes split into cellular/neutrophil defects (HIV, transplant, chemo, CGD) and humoral/splenic ones (XLA, CVID, sickle cell).

checks.q: Which condition causes neutrophil-related opportunistic infections?
checks.why: Chemo neutropenia and CGD affect phagocytes.

checks.q: Which is a cause of functional asplenia?
checks.why: Sickle cell autoinfarcts the spleen → encapsulated bacteria risk.

II-28.explain: Neutropenia → bacteria and moulds; T-cell loss → Pneumocystis, CMV, Cryptococcus; no antibody/spleen → encapsulated bacteria.

checks.q: Classic mould infection in prolonged neutropenia?
checks.why: Neutrophils fight Aspergillus; Cryptococcus/PCP reflect T-cell loss.

checks.q: Which organism suggests a T-cell defect?
checks.why: PJP reflects T-cell deficiency.

checks.q: Asplenia predisposes mainly to which organisms?
checks.why: Spleen and antibody clear encapsulated bacteria.

II-28.explain: Neutropenic patients cannot mount inflammation, so fever may be the only sign. Each opportunist has a signature.

checks.q: In febrile neutropenia, the only sign of sepsis may be?
checks.why: Without neutrophils, no pus or localising signs, just fever.

checks.q: Lab clue suggesting PJP pneumonia?
checks.why: High LDH with fever, dry cough and hypoxia.

checks.q: Typical eye manifestation of CMV in immunodeficiency?
checks.why: CMV retinitis (and colitis); Cryptococcus causes meningitis.

II-28.explain: Febrile neutropenia is defined by temperature and absolute neutrophil count, then cultures from all lumens. PJP needs BAL; CMV retinitis happens at very low CD4.

checks.q: Neutrophil threshold for febrile neutropenia?
checks.why: ≥38°C with neutrophils <0.5 × 10⁹/L; take line and peripheral cultures.

checks.q: CD4 count at which CMV retinitis typically occurs?
checks.why: CD4 ≤ 50; PJP risk starts at ≤ 200.

II-28.explain: Empirical antipseudomonal cover within an hour saves lives in neutropenic fever. PJP: co-trimoxazole, steroids if hypoxic. Toxo and VZV have specific agents.
II-28.hook: Febrile neutropenia: tazocin in the golden hour.

checks.q: First-line empirical antibiotic in febrile neutropenia?
checks.why: Antipseudomonal pip-taz within 1 hour; add vancomycin for line/instability.

checks.q: When are steroids added in PJP?
checks.why: Steroids if PaO2 ≤ 70 mmHg reduce mortality.

checks.q: Treatment of toxoplasmosis?
checks.why: Pyrimethamine with sulfadiazine; varicella gets IV aciclovir.

II-29.explain: Non-suppurative means immune-mediated, not direct infection: ARF and PSGN follow GAS after a latent period.

checks.q: Which are non-suppurative sequelae of GAS?
checks.why: ARF and PSGN are immune-mediated; quinsy is suppurative.

II-29.explain: ARF follows only throat infection (2-4 weeks); PSGN can follow throat (1-2 weeks) or skin (3-6 weeks).

checks.q: Latent period between GAS pharyngitis and ARF?
checks.why: ARF follows pharyngitis by 2-4 weeks.

checks.q: Latent period after GAS skin infection before PSGN?
checks.why: Skin 3-6 weeks; pharyngitis 1-2 weeks.

II-29.explain: ARF is molecular mimicry (antibodies to M protein hit heart, joints, brain). PSGN is immune-complex deposition consuming complement.

checks.q: Mechanism of acute rheumatic fever?
checks.why: Antibodies to M protein cross-react (type II HSR).

checks.q: Complement finding in PSGN?
checks.why: Immune complexes consume C3 via alternative pathway.

II-29.explain: Jones major criteria spell JONES. Carditis hits the mitral valve. PSGN gives a nephritic picture.
II-29.hook: J♥NES: Joints, Heart, Nodules, Erythema marginatum, Sydenham.

checks.q: Typical joint pattern in ARF?
checks.why: Migratory polyarthritis of large joints.

checks.q: Valve most commonly affected in rheumatic heart disease?
checks.why: Mitral: acute regurgitation, chronic fish-mouth stenosis.

checks.q: Classic urine colour in PSGN?
checks.why: Cola urine with periorbital oedema, hypertension, oliguria.

II-29.explain: Jones needs evidence of GAS plus criteria. Aschoff bodies are pathognomonic. PSGN low C3 should normalise by 8 weeks; if not, think another GN.

checks.q: Jones criteria require which combination plus GAS evidence?
checks.why: 2 major, or 1 major + 2 minor, plus ASO/anti-DNase B.

checks.q: Pathognomonic histology of rheumatic carditis?
checks.why: Aschoff bodies with Anitschkow cells.

checks.q: By when should C3 normalise in PSGN?
checks.why: Within 8 weeks; persistence suggests MPGN or lupus.

II-29.explain: Eradicate GAS, control inflammation, then long-term penicillin prophylaxis to prevent recurrence. PSGN is supportive; antibiotics don't prevent it.

checks.q: Eradication therapy in ARF?
checks.why: Penicillin V for 10 days; macrolides if anaphylaxis.

checks.q: Secondary prophylaxis after ARF?
checks.why: Benzathine penicillin IM every 3-4 weeks prevents recurrences.

checks.q: Do antibiotics for strep throat prevent PSGN?
checks.why: They prevent ARF but not PSGN.

II-30.explain: Pertussis symptoms come from toxins, not invasion, which is why the cough outlasts the bacteria.

checks.q: Organism causing whooping cough?
checks.why: Bordetella pertussis; toxin-mediated disease.

II-30.explain: Extremely contagious droplets; immunity wanes, so adolescents and adults with mild cough infect infants.

checks.q: Gram stain description of Bordetella pertussis?
checks.why: Aerobic gram-negative coccobacillus; attack rate >80%.

checks.q: Common source of infant pertussis?
checks.why: Waning immunity in adolescents/adults makes them the reservoir.

II-30.explain: Adhesins attach; tracheal cytotoxin kills ciliated cells. Pertussis toxin raises cAMP, trapping lymphocytes in blood; extreme counts sludge in pulmonary vessels.

checks.q: Which toxin kills ciliated cells?
checks.why: Tracheal cytotoxin destroys ciliated cells → violent cough.

checks.q: Pertussis toxin acts by disabling which protein?
checks.why: Disabling Gi raises cAMP → lymphocytosis, hypoglycaemia.

checks.q: Lymphocyte level linked to leukostasis and pulmonary hypertension?
checks.why: Lymphocytes >30 × 10⁹/L cause leukostasis.

II-30.explain: Catarrhal stage looks like a cold yet is most infectious; then paroxysms with whoop. Young infants often present with apnoea instead.

checks.q: Which pertussis stage is most infectious?
checks.why: Catarrhal stage, when it looks like a cold.

checks.q: Typical presentation in infants under 6 months?
checks.why: Apnoea/cyanosis, often no whoop.

II-30.explain: PCR is most sensitive early; culture needs special media. Marked lymphocytosis supports it.

checks.q: Preferred early diagnostic test for pertussis?
checks.why: NP swab PCR early; culture on Regan-Lowe/Bordet-Gengou.

checks.q: Typical FBC finding in pertussis?
checks.why: Pertussis toxin causes marked lymphocytosis.

II-30.explain: Macrolides shorten infectivity if given early. Azithromycin is safest in neonates. Young infants are admitted; contacts get prophylaxis. Maternal Tdap protects newborns.
II-30.hook: Tdap in pregnancy protects the newborn.

checks.q: Preferred antibiotic for pertussis in neonates?
checks.why: Azithromycin; erythromycin carries pyloric stenosis risk.

checks.q: Who receives prophylactic macrolides?
checks.why: All close contacts, regardless of vaccine status.

checks.q: Vaccine given in pregnancy to protect infants?
checks.why: Tdap in pregnancy; DTaP at 2, 4, 6 months.

II-31.explain: Salmonella causes two clinically distinct illnesses: NTS gastroenteritis and systemic typhoid fever.

checks.q: Typhoid is also called what?
checks.why: Typhoid = enteric fever, systemic Salmonella infection.

II-31.explain: NTS lives in animals (poultry, reptiles) and needs a big dose; typhoid lives only in humans.

checks.q: Classic pet associated with non-typhoidal Salmonella?
checks.why: Reptiles like turtles; also raw chicken/eggs, unpasteurised milk.

checks.q: Reservoir of Salmonella Typhi?
checks.why: Humans are the only reservoir.

II-31.explain: Salmonella is a motile, H2S-producing, non-lactose fermenter. Typhi invades Peyer patches, survives in macrophages and causes ulcer perforation by week 3.

checks.q: Lab feature distinguishing Salmonella from Shigella?
checks.why: Salmonella produces H₂S; both are non-lactose fermenters.

checks.q: When does intestinal perforation typically occur in typhoid?
checks.why: Peyer patch necrosis → perforation in week 3.

II-31.explain: NTS gives inflammatory diarrhoea; in sickle cell it seeds bone. Typhoid gives stepwise fever with relatively slow pulse and rose spots.

checks.q: Classic Salmonella complication in sickle cell disease?
checks.why: Salmonella osteomyelitis is characteristic in sickle cell.

checks.q: Pulse finding in typhoid?
checks.why: Relative bradycardia despite fever, plus rose spots.

II-31.explain: NTS stays in the gut (stool culture); typhoid is bacteraemic early (blood culture), with marrow most sensitive.

checks.q: Diagnostic test for non-typhoidal Salmonella enterocolitis?
checks.why: Stool culture; NTS stays largely in the gut.

checks.q: Most sensitive culture site for typhoid?
checks.why: Bone marrow; blood culture in week 1, leucopenia typical.

II-31.explain: Antibiotics prolong carriage in uncomplicated NTS, so they're reserved for high-risk children. Typhoid always needs antibiotics.

checks.q: Effect of antibiotics in uncomplicated NTS?
checks.why: They prolong carriage, so supportive care is preferred.

checks.q: Which child with NTS needs antibiotics?
checks.why: Under 3 months, immunocompromised, sickle cell or invasive disease.

checks.q: Treatment of XDR typhoid?
checks.why: Carbapenem for XDR; otherwise ceftriaxone or azithromycin.

II-32.explain: Small mutations (drift) cause seasonal epidemics; swapping whole gene segments (shift) creates novel viruses and pandemics.

checks.q: Antigenic shift causes what?
checks.why: Shift (reassortment) → pandemics; drift → epidemics.

II-32.explain: Children shed lots of virus and spread it. Those with chronic disease or on aspirin are high risk.

checks.q: Who are the main spreaders of influenza?
checks.why: Children shed more virus for longer.

checks.q: Which medication makes a child high risk with influenza?
checks.why: Aspirin (risk of Reye syndrome).

II-32.explain: HA binds sialic acid for entry; NA cleaves it to release progeny. Destroyed airway epithelium invites secondary bacterial pneumonia.
II-32.hook: HA hooks on, NA lets go.

checks.q: Function of neuraminidase?
checks.why: NA cleaves sialic acid to release virions; HA binds it.

checks.q: Why does secondary bacterial pneumonia follow influenza?
checks.why: Destroyed ciliated cells leave a denuded airway.

II-32.explain: Abrupt systemic onset; infants may look septic. Influenza B classically causes calf myositis. Improvement then deterioration suggests bacterial pneumonia.

checks.q: Typical onset of influenza?
checks.why: Abrupt fever, myalgia, dry cough.

checks.q: Influenza B classically causes which muscle problem?
checks.why: Calf myositis; also associated with Guillain-Barré.

II-32.explain: In season, diagnosis is clinical; PCR is reserved for those needing admission or high-risk.

checks.q: Test for hospitalised children with suspected influenza?
checks.why: PCR on NP swab; otherwise clinical diagnosis in season.

II-32.explain: Treat symptoms without aspirin. Neuraminidase inhibitors work best early. Vaccinate yearly from 6 months; first-timers under 9 need two doses.

checks.q: Antipyretic to avoid in influenza?
checks.why: Aspirin risks Reye syndrome.

checks.q: Ideal time window to start oseltamivir?
checks.why: Within 48 hours of onset for high-risk/severe cases.

checks.q: Vaccine doses for a 5-year-old's first influenza vaccination?
checks.why: Under 9 first time: two doses 4 weeks apart.

II-33.explain: Newborn care covers routine checks plus the transition from placental to independent breathing, circulation and thermoregulation.

checks.q: Disorders of newborn adaptation relate to what transition?
checks.why: The transition to extrauterine life.

II-33.explain: Adaptation disorders affect lungs, circulation, heat and glucose. Hypoglycaemia risk is high in babies with low reserves or high insulin.

checks.q: Which is an adaptation disorder of the newborn?
checks.why: TTN, PPHN, hypothermia, hypoglycaemia, jaundice.

checks.q: Which newborn is at highest risk of hypoglycaemia?
checks.why: Fetal hyperinsulinism persists after birth.

II-33.explain: Labour catecholamines activate ENaC to absorb lung fluid; C-section skips this, causing TTN. Brown fat makes heat via UCP1.

checks.q: Channel that clears fetal lung fluid at birth?
checks.why: Labour catecholamines activate ENaC; TTN = delayed clearance.

checks.q: Source of non-shivering thermogenesis in newborns?
checks.why: Brown fat uncoupling protein 1.

II-33.explain: TTN is classic after elective C-section. Jaundice in the first day is never physiological. Cephalohaematoma is subperiosteal so it respects sutures.

checks.q: Classic scenario for TTN?
checks.why: Term C-section baby with grunting.

checks.q: Jaundice appearing when is always pathological?
checks.why: Within 24 h; also cephalohaematoma does not cross sutures.

II-33.explain: Apgar scores track adaptation; a full exam within 72 h. Routine screens include oximetry, hearing and blood spot. A pre/post-ductal gap means right-to-left ductal shunting.

checks.q: Deadline for the newborn physical examination?
checks.why: Within 72 h (repeated at 6-8 weeks).

checks.q: Which is a routine newborn screen?
checks.why: Pulse oximetry, hearing and heel-prick blood spot.

checks.q: Pre-/post-ductal saturation gap suggests?
checks.why: Right-to-left ductal shunt in PPHN.

II-33.explain: Keep warm and dry, delay cord clamping, encourage skin-to-skin and breastfeeding. Vitamin K prevents haemorrhagic disease.

checks.q: Recommended minimum delay before cord clamping?
checks.why: Delay cord clamping ≥60 s.

checks.q: Routine vitamin K dose at birth?
checks.why: 1 mg IM prevents vitamin K deficiency bleeding.

checks.q: First step for asymptomatic neonatal hypoglycaemia?
checks.why: Feed, then dextrose gel, then IV dextrose.

II-34.explain: RDS is surfactant deficiency; surfactant reaches mature levels around week 35, so earlier babies are at risk.

checks.q: Week around which surfactant reaches mature levels?
checks.why: Around week 35 per notes.

II-34.explain: Prematurity is the key risk. Fetal insulin in diabetic pregnancy inhibits surfactant; C-section skips labour stress.

checks.q: Most important risk factor for RDS?
checks.why: Prematurity; diabetes (fetal insulin) and C-section add risk.

II-34.explain: Surfactant from type II pneumocytes lowers surface tension; without it small alveoli collapse per Laplace (P = 2T/r).
II-34.hook: Laplace: small r, big collapse pressure.

checks.q: Cells that produce surfactant?
checks.why: Type II pneumocytes.

checks.q: Main consequence of inadequate surfactant?
checks.why: Alveoli fail to open → poor oxygenation.

II-34.explain: Distress starts within hours of birth and worsens as alveoli collapse.

checks.q: RDS signs typically appear within how long of birth?
checks.why: Within 4 h: tachypnoea, grunting, flaring, recession.

II-34.explain: CXR shows diffuse atelectasis with air bronchograms. Amniotic L:S ratio ≥ 2 indicates maturity.

checks.q: Typical chest X-ray in RDS?
checks.why: Ground-glass, air bronchograms, low volumes; fissure fluid = TTN.

checks.q: L:S ratio indicating lung maturity?
checks.why: L:S ≥ 2 indicates mature lungs.

II-34.explain: Antenatal steroids accelerate surfactant. CPAP from birth, surfactant if oxygen need rises above 30%. Prematurity complications include NEC, ROP, BPD.

checks.q: Best prevention of RDS in threatened preterm labour?
checks.why: Maternal steroids accelerate surfactant maturation.

checks.q: FiO₂ threshold for giving surfactant on CPAP?
checks.why: Surfactant if FiO₂ >0.30.

checks.q: Drug used for apnoea of prematurity?
checks.why: Caffeine citrate.

II-35.explain: Meconium passage is a term/post-term phenomenon, so MAS affects mature babies.

checks.q: MAS typically affects which infants?
checks.why: Term and post-term infants.

II-35.explain: Fetal stress triggers meconium. In a preterm, meconium is unusual and suggests Listeria.

checks.q: Main risk factor for meconium aspiration?
checks.why: Post-term, IUGR, pre-eclampsia, oligohydramnios.

checks.q: Meconium-stained liquor in a preterm suggests?
checks.why: Listeria monocytogenes infection.

II-35.explain: Hypoxia relaxes the anal sphincter and boosts peristalsis. Meconium causes ball-valve trapping, inactivates surfactant and triggers PPHN.

checks.q: Trigger for fetal meconium passage?
checks.why: Hypoxia → peristalsis + sphincter relaxation.

checks.q: Mechanism causing pneumothorax in MAS?
checks.why: Partial obstruction traps air → rupture.

II-35.explain: Stained skin and nails, distress from birth, overinflated chest. Air leaks are common.

checks.q: Typical chest shape in MAS?
checks.why: Hyperinflation → barrel chest.

checks.q: Frequency of air leak in MAS?
checks.why: Pneumothorax in 10-20%.

II-35.explain: CXR shows patchy infiltrates with hyperinflation (unlike RDS low volumes). Saturation gap flags PPHN.
II-35.hook: MAS: big lungs; RDS: small lungs.

checks.q: CXR in MAS?
checks.why: Coarse patchy infiltrates with hyperinflation, flattened diaphragms.

checks.q: Pre-/post-ductal saturation gap in MAS indicates?
checks.why: Right-to-left ductal shunt of PPHN.

II-35.explain: Current guidance: no routine tracheal suction; ventilate within a minute. NICU support including surfactant and iNO; ECMO if refractory.

checks.q: Initial approach to a non-vigorous meconium-stained baby?
checks.why: No routine suctioning; ventilate within the first minute.

checks.q: Treatment for PPHN in MAS?
checks.why: iNO dilates pulmonary vessels.

checks.q: Last-resort therapy for refractory MAS?
checks.why: ECMO if refractory to ventilation and iNO.
